proposed_edges.relationship: Brenner and Isett challenge Pomeranz through social-property relations (2002); Broadberry and Gupta place the advanced parts of Asia with Europe’s stagnating periphery on wages and prices (2006); Allen and colleagues dispute Chinese–English urban real-wage parity (2011); Broadberry, Guan and Li place divergence between leading regions around 1700 (2021)
proposed_edges.map_label: Property relations, wages and regional GDP, 2002–2021
proposed_edges.evidence_note: This arrow represents four named interventions, not a verdict of the economic-history entry, which includes Pomeranz and his allies; each establishes something different. Brenner and Isett (JAS 61:2, 2002; online reprint read in part, no folios), on social-property relations: England's divergence came from "this already existing decisive divergence, not England’s capacity to gain access to the American colonies"; the delta followed "a Malthusian pattern", England "a Smithian pattern"; "Contra Pomeranz". Broadberry and Gupta (EHR 59:1, 2006; summary and pp. 2–3 read by the second research pass), on wages and prices: "Contrary to the claims of Pomeranz, Parthasarathi, and other 'world historians', the prosperous parts of Asia between 1500 and 1800 look similar to the stagnating southern, central, and eastern parts of Europe … The 'great divergence' … was already well underway before 1800" (p. 2). Allen, Bassino, Ma, Moll-Murata and van Zanden (EHR 2011, read pp. 8–9, 29–31), on urban real wages: "our findings also dispute the revisionists’ claim that the advanced parts of China, such as the Yangzi Delta, were on a par with England"; "Adam Smith’s pessimism looks closer to the truth than the revisionists’ optimism" (p. 31); they also find Chinese urban wages on a par with central and southern Europe, against the "rise of the west" literature (pp. 30–31). Broadberry, Guan and Li (JEH 2021, read pp. 958–959), on regional GDP per capita: "The Great Divergence thus began around 1700, earlier than originally suggested by the California School, but later than implied by earlier writers" (p. 958). The qualified chronology is theirs alone. None endorses Huang's involution, whose dispute with Pomeranz is drawn on its own arrows. Robert Brenner is not yet an atlas entry; if he becomes one, his critique with Isett moves to its own arrow.

proposed_edges.relationship: Historical scales and teaching after the nation: world history as comparison that tests “the universality or regional specificity of particular processes”, against curricula still organised by nation (AHA presidential address, 2014)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: His AHA presidential address, delivered 3 January 2014 and published in AHR 119:1 (2014), 1–22, read via WebFetch extraction of the AHA text (no pagination; the last fifth not covered). World history "makes comparisons that interrogate claims about the universality or regional specificity of particular processes"; he asks "how our discipline is responding and might respond to the changing geography of our own era"; in a survey of "218 AHA member departments", "46 percent of all classes" at the introductory level "were on national histories"; he warns that "most global history narratives thus far have been strongly materialistic, and focused on general processes"; and closes on "reframing for a less national age". A later programme statement, distinct from the 2000 method on edge_898.

proposed_edges.relationship: Consumer demand compared across Eurasian cores: sugar, cloth and “consumerist” attitudes in China, Japan and western Europe, with differences “small and of uncertain direction” (2000)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: His own summary of chapters 3–4 in the introduction (2000, pp. 17–18; read by both research passes): Part 2 "begins by moving away from survival-oriented activities to examine new kinds of consumer demand"; differences "in both quantities of goods available and 'consumerist' attitudes among these societies seem small and of uncertain direction. (For instance, mid-eighteenth-century Chinese almost certainly consumed more sugar than Europeans, and people in the Lower Yangzi core may have produced as much cloth per capita in 1750 as Britons did in 1800.)" The chapters themselves are unread. Contested by Huang (2002, p. 521, as the second pass reads it) and answered by Pomeranz (2003, p. 168: "probably the bottom 75 percent of the Jiangnan population lived at least as well as their English counterparts").

proposed_edges.relationship: Wallerstein’s world-system grouped with the “Europe-centered stories” whose motor is western Europe’s prior advantages; Pomeranz borrows from them but argues for a late, contingent divergence (2000)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: His own introduction (2000, pp. 14–16; read by both research passes). Braudel, Wallerstein and Chaudhuri appear with North in "a second group of arguments" that "emphasize the emergence of institutions in early modern Europe" (p. 14); "the motor of Wallerstein’s story is western Europe’s unique combination of relatively free labor, large and productive urban populations, and merchants and governments" (p. 15, as the second pass quotes it); "This work borrows from these arguments—mostly those of the various 'institutionalists'—but ultimately argues for different propositions" (p. 16). A bounded critique of a Eurocentric premise, not a rejection of unequal exchange: he cites Williams, Frank and Amin as earlier arguments from colonial extraction (p. 3 n. 2). The chapter discussions are unread.

edges_considered_not_proposed.reason: Brenner is not yet an atlas entry; Brenner and Isett stay inside the economic → kenneth_pomeranz critique as named critics.
The NLR essay is read at its opening only.

new_sources.citation: Robert Brenner and Christopher Isett, “England’s Divergence from China’s Yangzi Delta: Property Relations, Microeconomics, and Patterns of Development,” Journal of Asian Studies 61, no. 2 (May 2002): 609–662.

verification.note: Read in part for revision 1.144 (data/extension-2026/post2000-wave1-2026-10-17/evidence-pomeranz.md §1c) in the International Socialism online reprint (posted 3 November 2004, "From The Journal of Asian Studies 61, no. 2, May 2002"); no print pagination, and the reprint breaks off mid-sentence. Read: the opening, "Pomeranz’s Argument", their thesis and the first sections on social-property relations. In Brenner and Isett's summary, Pomeranz attributes the divergence to "access to the land, raw materials, and above all slave labor, of its American colonies"; "The burden of our critique is that, from the dawn of the early modern period, the institutional framework or system of social-property relations that structured the English economy was radically different … from that of the Yangzi delta"; "It was this already existing decisive divergence, not England’s capacity to gain access to the American colonies … that explains why the two economies distanced themselves"; the delta followed "a Malthusian pattern", England "a Smithian pattern"; "Contra Pomeranz"; landlord extraction is "a major rentier element … that Pomeranz ignores". Their delta evidence draws heavily on Huang (1985, 1990, 1996). Pages to be cited from the JAS print before release.
